blocks.heading: Where a key comes from
text: Nora needs somewhere for Caleb's €4,150 to land. Her wallet makes her a key in under a millisecond and does not ask her anything.
Everything she owns now rests on one word in that sentence.

blocks.heading: It is not a password
text: There is no account, no server, nobody to register with. A private key is **256 random bits**. That is the entire object.

blocks.label: what a private key looks like (illustrative)

blocks.heading: Almost any number will do
text: The key has to be at least 1 and less than the curve's order $n$. Bitcoin's curve, secp256k1, fixes that number in the standard:

blocks.caption: Just under $2^{256}$. About $2^{-127}$ of random draws land outside the range - a wallet redraws, and in practice never has to.

blocks.question: Nobody registers Nora's key anywhere, so nothing stops another wallet from drawing the same 256 bits. Why is that not a real risk?
answer: Take a billion keys - more than every wallet ever created. The chance that any two of them collide is around one in $10^{59}$.
The safety does not come from a registry. It comes from the space being far too large to land in twice.

blocks.heading: So where do the bits come from?
text: Not from the wallet. It asks the operating system, which keeps a pool stirred by timing jitter, interrupts, and on modern hardware a dedicated noise circuit.
The wallet is a thin caller. The quality of Nora's key is decided entirely by that pool.

blocks.heading: The line someone removed
text: A Debian maintainer patched OpenSSL to silence a memory-checker warning. The patched line fed uninitialised memory into the random pool.
It also happened to be feeding in everything else. What was left seeding the generator was the **process ID**.

blocks.alt: Three bars whose length is the number of bits: 15, 128 and 256, with the 15-bit bar almost invisible
blocks.caption: Linux caps process IDs at 32,768. Every key that build could produce fits in a **32,768-row table**.

blocks.title: Not a search - a lookup
text: For twenty months, from September 2006 to the advisory, that build shipped. Anyone could generate all 32,768 keys in advance and simply check whether yours was one of them.
These were SSH and TLS keys; bitcoin did not exist yet. The failure mode is what carries over, not the victims.

blocks.heading: People are worse than a broken PRNG
text: Some early users skipped randomness on purpose: hash a memorised phrase, call it a wallet, keep nothing on disk.
Attackers pre-computed keys for every phrase they could think of and watched the chain. Funds arrived and left within minutes.

blocks.heading: Where this breaks, permanently
text: A key drawn from 15 bits and a key drawn from 256 bits are both 32-byte strings. Nothing you can measure on the key itself tells them apart.
Randomness cannot be audited after the fact. That is why the standards test the _generator_ - NIST SP 800-90A for the construction, 800-90B for the noise source - and never the number that comes out.

blocks.heading: One sentence worth keeping
text: A key is not strong because it is long. It is strong because the process that made it had somewhere unpredictable to draw from.
Nora's 256 bits are now a secret. Next: how the same number turns into something she can safely email to Caleb.
